thread.title: Seeing Is Believing - A Review Of AudioEye's Prospects And Undervalued Stock - AudioEye, Inc. (NASDAQ:AEYE)

author: Mark Hake
title: Seeing Is Believing - A Review Of AudioEye's Prospects And Undervalued Stock - AudioEye, Inc. (NASDAQ:AEYE)
text:
AudioEye, Inc. ( AEYE ) is a fast growing SaaS B-to-B niche technology company. It sells software which make corporate and government websites friendly for people with disabilities. Helping these people see, hear and touch the Internet is a niche field in which no public company other than AEYE is solely focused. Corporations and government entities are increasingly willing to pay AEYE to “make websites accessible”. AEYE has a “moat” so to speak and is profiting greatly.
Source: www.audioeye.com (The “Man in Blue” stick figure on the lower right of a website is a sign it’s AEYE enabled.)
I like this stock because AEYE has plenty of catalysts and enough net cash on its balance sheet to cover the cash burn until free cash flow occurs in 2020. AEYE is significantly undervalued. My target price is over 60% higher than today’s price. First, let’s look at AEYE’s business.
The Business of Helping People with Disabilities to Surf the Web AEYE’s niche business is a demand pull and supply push play at the same time.
Demand Pull . Corporations are willing to re-mediate their websites for accessibility. Demand is growing for one simple reason: It’s good business. Accenture recently came out with a report titled “The Disability Inclusion Advantage: Companies that improve disability inclusion over time outperform their peers.” They point out that 1 billion people are estimated to have disabilities worldwide. (AEYE claims 15% of the world have some form of disability in their investor presentation, but there are 7.53 billion in the world, so this ratio is closer to 13%). The Accenture report says there are 15.1 million people in the U.S. at working age with disabilities. The St. Louis Fed reports there are a total of 206 million working age people (aged 15-64) in the U.S as of September. That makes the disability ratio about 7.3% of the U.S. working age population. Granted, corporations don’t just sell their services to working age people. The Accenture report sites research from the American Institutes for Research (April 2018) and the U.S. Office of Disability Employment Policy that disabled people are the third largest U.S. market segment with over $21 billion in discretionary income:
The Accenture report reports that corporations that act in this field earn higher corporate returns and stock prices. This is a virtual selling tool for AEYE.
Source: Accenture Report, “The Disability Inclusion Advantage”
Supply Push : What AEYE offers is unique. This can be seen online with a number of videos. Some Vimeo videos describe AEYE products, such as “The Man in Blue” , “About AudioEye” , “Online Demonstration of the AudioEye Accessibilty Solution” (sic) . This last video is a user’s description of how AEYE’s products work. There are also some YouTube videos (but don’t watch the German music group AudioEye videos), including an interesting car dealer video. Apparently a lot of car dealer sites are now using AEYE’s products.
AEYE offers a JavaScript solution for html script in websites, which interjects alternate text, hearing solutions, toolbars, and content system fixes. When you click on the AudioEye "Man in Blue" icon, a vertical toolbar pops up on the right hand side of the AEYE enabled site. You don't have to download anything. AEYE's solutions make sites accessible in four ways: (1) visual fixes, including color blindness, font-size changes, etc., (2) auditory and audio files (close captioning and scripting) fixes, (3) mobility issues (including navigation without using a mouse, voice-based navigation, and (4) cognitive challenges (dyslexia, etc.) fixes.
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) has created a sort of demand pull and supply push for AEYE's solutions. While the ADA doesn’t mandate immediate website compliance, there seems to be a checklist that some law firms claim the ADA requires for the visually impaired to be able to read a site. An increasing number of companies are being sued for ADA compliance. AEYE recently published a investor presentation which has a chart showing the huge increase in such lawsuits:
Source: AEYE investor presentation 11-2-18 available on www.audioeye.com
This is good for AEYE. It drives business to them. AEYE published a whitepaper, “Guide for Addressing ADA Legal Demand Letters” that addresses the issue of how to handle these lawsuits. The essence of these demand letters is that the accused companies are out of compliance with a World Wide Web Consortium’s recommendation called “Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.0 ” (or WCAG 2.0 AA). These standards have also been incorporated into an ISO standard, but none of these are actual U.S. law. Plaintiff law firms have been filing suits claiming that ADA standards are being violated if a corporation's website does not conform to the WCAG guidelines. The ADA was passed in 1990 well before the Internet, but the Justice Department has yet to pass any regulations on website compliance for non-public entities. Here is a law firm’s discussion of the court cases which have sided for and against ADA website compliance. Nevertheless, the suits and court cases feed demand and supply for AEYE’s products, especially since AEYE offers a form of certification to show that a site is compliant by using AEYE solutions. Here is what AEYE says about ADA compliance, in its 10-K:
Source: 10-K Report 2017 AudioEye, Inc.
AEYE points out in the 10-K that “there are 6 million businesses (666,000 public and private employers) that must comply with ADA laws.” It also indicates there are two laws that require government agency websites to be compliant, including the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and the Twenty First Century Communication and Video Accessibility Act of 2010. AEYE says that since the last Act was passed a growing number of mandates from agencies including the Department of Justice have been pointing to the WCAG 2.0 standard as indicating compliance for agency websites.
AEYE has pretty good patents protecting its solutions. None of them seems to have been challenged to date. It has six U.S. patents in two patent families, and four or five in application, along with 5 trademarks and several pending. AEYE also not have any major competitors. A few consultants offer one-off services and some sites like www.complyfirst.com and www.siteimprove.com that offering automated testing and reporting on ADA compliance issues of corporation's website. But none offer the type of actual solutions, certification and compliance test products that AEYE offers. AEYE indicated to me that some of these competitors, although good at marketing, lose their clients to AEYE because they don't necessarily solve the clients' site problems. A number of the companies offering solutions in the ADA website compliance area are partnered with AEYE, such as www.kasasa.com . AEYE claims to have over 400 banks which use its services as a result of the marketing of these kind of companies. No public company is solely focused on this area other than AEYE.
Sales . From 2015 on, AEYE restructured itself and started selling its B-to-B software on a cloud-based Subscription-as-a-Service (SaaS) basis. AEYE sells through direct and increasingly through indirect channels, or resellers, such as large platform providers like NetSuite (Oracle), which AEYE just signed. AEYE targets 4 verticals: education, government, retail and financials (banks). The company is focusing on scaling its revenue mainly by focusing on large content management system providers (CMS). These CMS partners have hundreds and thousands of websites under their purvue. Although AEYE pays a commission to these large CMS and other resellers, AEYE gains by having a much lower cost of acquisition and lower software install costs. AEYE can standardize the installations in these large numbers of corporate websites sold through indirect partners. Recently AEYE reveled its direct vs. indirect client totals and sample client names in its investor presentation dated November 2, 2018. This presentation appears to be only available on AEYE's website (no public SEC filing):
Source: AEYE Investor Presentation 11-2-18 ( www.audioeye.com )
These two charts show that AEYE is dramatically growing its client base through these indirect sales channels. During the recent quarterly call, management indicated it has 14 channel partners with a potential to reach over 78,000 websites. The first slide above indicates AEYE expects to have 996 clients by year end. So by combining these two facts revealed by AEYE, we can project their growth in terms of client numbers. Let's say AEYE will grow from roughly 1,000 accounts by 2018 year end to over 78,000 websites with just its 14 channel partners over some period of time. Let's assume that the average account has 1.5 websites. That means AEYE can reach 52,000 accounts using these channel partners. That is a 52 fold increase. Let's also assume it takes between four and five years for AEYE to achieve only a 50% successful sell-through rate with these partners:
Source: Hake estimates
The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) will likely be between 92 - 125% (per year) in new client contract accounts. Over a shorter period, the CAGR should be even higher.
Forecasting Sales . AEYE reports two items in its financial statements which allow the astute investor to forecast future sales. These are "Deferred Revenue" and "Contract Amount in Excess of Deferred and Recognized Revenue." In most cases after AEYE signs a contract it doesn’t recognize any item on its statements under GAAP until it sends out an invoice to the client for a one year period, even though the contract may obligate the client to pay for services over several years. So that remaining balance, which is not billed to the client because it is customary to invoice or bill no longer than a year at a time, becomes an off-balance sheet item called "Excess of Deferred and Recognized Revenue."
Here is how the accounting works. When the invoice is sent out by AEYE to a client for a 1 year period, a debit entry is made which increases Accounts Receivable, and a credit entry is also made for the same amount which increases the liability account called Deferred Revenue. This is for the 1 year amount of the invoice, even though the required client payments may be made quarterly or monthly. Once AEYE performs its service and gets paid monthly or quarterly, it debits (increases) the Cash Account for the amount of the payment. But but it only reduces the Deferred Revenue liability account (with a debit) and increases the Recognized Revenue Account (with a credit) for the amount of the year for which work was done and paid for (monthly or quarterly). The whole 2nd or 3rd year portion of the contract, which is still not billed, is not on the balance sheet but displays in the Notes as "Excess Amount over Recognized and Deferred Revenue. In effect, these amounts are Unbilled Receivables. Here is a hypothetical example how it works:
Source: Hake
This shows that over four quarters in Yr 1, four new contracts are booked, one each a quarter. The new Contract amount "booked" each quarter is either billed (as either Recognized Revenue or Deferred Revenue) for a 1 year going forward period, or unbilled ("Excess" amount) for the remainder of the booked amount. As each quarter progresses, a draw-down from Deferred Revenue into Recognized Revenue occurs. But the unbilled amount (representing a 1 year period for the 2 year contracts, and a 2 year period for the 3 year contracts) stays the same during these first four quarters. As new contracts are booked each quarter, the unbilled or "Excess" amount increases. Starting in Year 2, a second "draw-down" effect will occur, where unbilled amounts from the "Excess" amounts are drawn into the two billed categories (which also draw-down from Deferred Revenue into Recognized Revenue). As sales accelerate and more contracts are added each quarter in Yr 2, the unbilled "Excess" amount will start to grow again. The point is that you can see that both the billed Deferred Revenue and the unbilled "Excess" amount are good indications of future sales from the two "draw-down" effects.
This is very important, since it allows us to use it as a metric to forecast future revenue of the company. Here is an example of this “Contract Excess” which is from the latest Q3 2018 10-Q report:
Source: AEYE 10-Q Report for Quarter Ending Sept. 30, 2018
This “Excess Amount” is an interesting metric since it shows that AEYE has $6.88 million which it has not recorded as either Deferred Revenue, Account Receivable or Revenue as of Sept. 30, 2018. Let’s think about that a little bit.
Most of AEYE’s contract sales are very sticky. We expect sales to be at least $5.5 million (on a recognized basis) for 2018. The company gave guidance in its press release that sales for 2018 would be between $5 and $6 million:
Source: Company Press Release dated 11-14-18
AEYE sells subscription software. Typically the term for direct sales are for one year and indirect sales seem to be for at least 2 or 3 years. What is a buyer going to do after his subscription runs out? Go to another seller? Redo the JavaScript tools in his website? Not likely. So for all practical purposes AEYE's contracts are "evergreen". These are powerful recurring revenues which likely do not have to be resold with a lot of expense even when the contract is finished.
Metrics . Therefore this increase in Excess Amount is a good metric to predict future sales. This year’s sales will be at least 50% that over the next two years since the $5.5 million expected this year will continue to be rolled over and the $6.5 million in Excess will be booked over the next 1 to 2 years. The press release guidance indicated that bookings will be between $11 million and $12 million by the end of the year.
I estimate that the amount of new contracts coming in next year, plus the recognition of at 40 - 50% of the increase in Excess Amount (i.e. bookings) will bring sales to $11 million in 2019 (or over double the 2018 amount). Since most indirect contracts seem to be for about two years, based on my discussions with management, we can take about half, less a certain amount that are for one year subscriptions. My estimate is that 45-47% of bookings will show up in Revenue each year. In addition, new contracts will be added and bookings will continue to grow in 2020. Here is my forecast, based on these ratios:
Source: Hake estimates
The key column here is the "Increase in Contracts". By 2020 year end, I estimate AEYE will be "booking" $44 million in fixed contracts. Assuming 45% - 47% of that will be recognized as Revenue, and the rest in a split between Deferred Revenue, which will show up as a liability, and Excess Amounts (see above), a non-balance sheet item and a good metric for future sales. Keep in mind that $47 million is AEYE's present stock market value. So you can see AEYE is very cheap (more on this later).
There is every reason to believe that this phenomenal growth in both Fixed Contracts and Sales will continue, based on AEYE’s history:
Source: AEYE SEC filings and Hake estimates
This table shows that Sales and Fixed Contracts have grown well over 100% in both categories for the past two years. This is from three effects:(1) Growth in bookings of new client contracts, (2) the recurring "draw-down" effects over time of existing contract subscriptions moving from billed Deferred Revenue and unbilled "Excess" amounts into Recognized Revenue, and (3) renewals of existing client contracts after their contract expires (the "evergreen" effect). These growth drivers, along with the company’s business “moat” as described above, add up to a very powerful business model.
Cash, Cash Flow and Catalysts . AEYE Has Plenty of Cash.
AEYE has $6.09 million in cash and cash equivalents. Its market cap is $47 million. That is 13.6% of its value. Most of the cash came from a $6.5 million private offering (apparently not a PIPE offering) in August 2018. It has no cash debt ($32K in convertible notes – but why haven’t they paid that off?). But there is the matter of Deferred Revenue. It appears on the balance sheet as $2.498 million. Technically it doesn’t need to be deducted from cash to derive Net Cash. GAAP requires Deferred Revenue to be recorded liability. It is not really a cash liability other than in the sense that if AEYE does not somehow perform on its contracts and then invoice its clients, accept the monthly subscription revenue (probably automatically on an ACH basis), the $2.5 million Deferred Revenue liability would have to be paid back to its customers. But that is not very likely to happen. Nevertheless, to be conservative, I deducted this liability from Net Cash. The Enterprise Value of AEYE (at $43 million) is lower than the Market Cap ($47 million):
Source: Hake
Net Cash, including the deduction for Deferred Revenue, is 7.6% of the company’s market cap. This is very attractive, as it provides a buffer for the company to continue to burn cash as it builds out its business. More importantly, the company is not going to need any more cash or capital raises. AEYE's 10-Q indicates AEYE does not plan to raise cash for the next 12 months. I confirmed this with Carr Bettis, the Executive Chairman. It also is confirmed by my assessment of the company's Free Cash Flow (FCF) below. Moreover, AEYE has over 1.8 million warrants with an average exercise price of $4.66 per share. These warrants are now in-the-money by $1.66 per share ($6.30 - $$.66 per share) and have an average life of over 2.2 years left to be exercised by the warrant holders. Theoretically this means over $8.7 million in proceeds would be paid to AEYE by the warrant holders after they exercise their warrants ($4.66 million x 1.8 million warrants). However, after discussion with the company, I estimate that at least 75% of the warrants (and options) have cash-less exercise features. This means AEYE would not receive 75% of the warrant cash proceeds upon exercise. But AEYE could still receive some portion of the remaining $2.2 million ($8.7 million * 0.25) proceeds in varying amounts over the next two years. Altogether, if the warrants were all converted today (since they are in-the-money), AEYE would have $8.2 million ($6 m cash + $2.2 million warrant proceeds) at its disposal, or over 17% of its market value.
Cash Flow
One of AEYE's key strengths is that SaaS revenue is not only recurring in nature, but it tends to have higher margins as the life of the contract continues and renews. Recently AEYE delved into this in its investor presentation:
Source: AEYE investor presentation 11-2-18 ( www.audioeye.com )
This chart shows that the ADP account has produced margins for AEYE of 83% at inception and it later grew to 90% three years later. GameStop's account at AEYE grew from 76% to 95% margins. Management indicated to me that this typical level of high margin is a major reason why AEYE should be cash flow positive as its growth continues. By the way, these margin numbers are awesome on an absolute basis. The average gross margin is 81% across its customer base, which is incredibly high.
Although AEYE will not be net cash flow positive next year, I think that is only by choice. I mean that in the sense that Amazon ( AMZN ) was cash flow negative many years, but effectively by choice. It didn't have to e xpand so aggressively. The same applies here with AEYE. The company is aggressively expanding and hiring sales force and implementation / software teams. AEYE could grow at a much slower rate, resulting in a much lower cash burn. But why should it? AEYE is pursuing a massive "land grab" expanding sales on a demand pull and supply push basis, as explained above, and has no real competition.
Nevertheless based on my model (which is included at the end of this article), I estimate that by 2020, AEYE will be significantly Free Cash Flow (FCF) positive, at least $5.8 million. That would represent a 12% FCF yield based on the company's present $47 million market value. In fact, 2019 could also turn out to be FCF positive, depending on its margins. We estimate 2019 will only be only -$502K negative.
Here is our estimate of the AEYE’s growth in Net Income, EBITDA and FCF:
Source: Hake estimates
Catalysts
The most prominent catalyst driving AEYE's business to date is the regulatory compliance factor as pointed out above. One key factor here is the Department of Justice (DOJ). If the DOJ decides to publish extensive regulations on ADA compliance for non-government entities, there will be an immediate and sustained massive windfall to AEYE. Although not likely under the Trump Administration, I suspect it will happen in the next three to five years. There are several other catalysts as well. Google ( GOOG ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), Samsung and a host of other large companies are all not only interested in improving their virtual assistant products, but are diving deeper into artificial intelligence. Google has a site discussing their accessibility initiatives and research, including their input on the WCAG standards. They are continuously interested in improving their products with accessibility and compliance. They are probably clearly aware of and looking at AEYE, either from a strategic standpoint or more. A third catalyst for the AEYE stock price is its float. Management and significant shareholders own about 40+% of the stock (more on this below). As sales and cash flow increase, this will squeeze the stock higher. My discussions with management indicate that they are not looking to sell at any kind of cheap valuation (again see below). A fourth catalyst is the natural aging of the baby boomer population. This is a significant growth driver for both sales and cash flow for AEYE. Valuation I believe that AEYE is substantially undervalued. Here is our assessment of its present value ratios:
As mentioned above, most of these ratios would be even more attractive if it weren't for management's aggressive sales push. Keep in mind that contracts I expect to be booked in 2020 will be equal to today's market cap, as shown above. That means AEYE is selling for only 1x my expected level of booked contracts by 2020. A more reasonable ratio, given the growth, recurring, draw-down and evergreen nature of contracts booked, would be 5 or 6x times that amount. Here is our estimate of AEYE's real value today:
Our target price of $10.14 is over 60% higher than today's price, and is conservative given AEYE's cash generation power. This is also in-line with some Street forecasts I have seen.
Low Risk . It seems that there is little downside risk, given the company's cash balance, its steady business profile and the large amount of management holdings. Note also that the company recently raised $6 million in equity capital at $6.25 per share this summer with institutional investors hosted by BRiley FBR (the only securities firm which follows AEYE). AEYE also completed an S-1 registration for those buyers' stock (and management warrants and options) this past quarter and listed the stock on NASDAQ's main exchange. Those institutional shareholders are not likely to sell anywhere near today's price. Here is our estimate of what the fully diluted structure looks like:
Source: AEYE SEC filings and Hake estimates
This table shows that between management, the 5%+ shareholders, and these new institutional investors, AEYE is in firm hands for over 51% of the fully diluted share holdings. Management owns about 24-25% of the common stock outright. Based on AEYE's recent S-1 and 10-Q filings I estimate that management owns about 42% of the warrants and options outstanding. The table above shows these represent 23.2% of the fully diluted shares. Therefore management probably controls about 34% of the company on a fully diluted basis. Combined with the recent institutional investors who paid $6.25 per share for 1 million shares (about 12% of the stock), almost 46% of the stock is in strong hands.
Risks to Consider Cash Burn: My estimate is that in 2018 AEYE will burn $1.8 million of operating cash flowcash. But the company has $6 million in cash and up to $2.2 million more including warrant exercise proceeds at its disposal to pay for this. Even if the company doesn't become FCF positive, or it takes longer than I estimate, AEYE should be able to afford to grow at this pace for at least 3 years . Retention: AEYE recently reported in its 11-2-18 presentation that it enjoys a 96% retention rate of its clients (the "evergreen effect"). More importantly, the presentation showed that AEYE's indirect contracts, which are growing as a percent of sales (see the table earlier above) are now much longer in duration than its direct channel contracts:
Source: AEYE investor presentation 11-2-18 ( www.audioeye.com )
So this means that not only are contracts lasting longer, but there is only a 4% or less chance they won't renew. So retention is not a big risk.
Legal and patent issues: AEYE is not involved in any lawsuits according to its filings, that have not been resolved. Based on our research we have not found any claims against the company's patents (see above). Conclusion I suggest investors buy AEYE at today's prices. The stock appears undervalued, and I target a price of $10.14 at a minimum. AEYE will likely track much higher than that price as year-over-year sales and contract growth remains at over 100% each quarter. The stock is worth at least 60% more than today's price.
